episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for Friday, April 17, 2026. And here's who is innovating in higher education today.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Insights and Trends today, Purdue University has become the first university in the United States to require A.I. literacy for graduation. According to Fast Company, the institution announced the requirement late last year, establishing a milestone in aligning higher education with an A.I. enabled workforce.

The approach centers on a three pillar framework. First, students learn about A.I., gaining hands-on experience with tools integrated into their fields of study while understanding both capabilities and limitations. Second, students learn with A.I., using it as a collaborative partner while maintaining responsibility for decisions and developing judgment through guided real-world practice. Third, students learn beyond A.I., reinforcing distinctly human skills like critical thinking, creativity, empathy, and ethical reasoning that machines cannot replicate.

The stakes are significant. According to the International Monetary Fund, A.I. will impact about sixty percent of jobs in advanced economies. The World Economic Forum ranks analytical thinking, resilience, flexibility, and agility among the most critical future workplace skills. Yet while more than ninety percent of companies plan increased A.I. spending within three years, only one percent say it's woven into everyday work. The gap between corporate A.I. intentions and workplace reality creates urgency for universities preparing students for careers that may not yet exist.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Turning to Beyond Ed, Anthropic has unveiled a new A.I. model called Mythos that the company says is too dangerous to release publicly. According to Scientific American, Mythos operates with senior level software engineering capabilities, identifying and exploiting software vulnerabilities. In testing, it discovered critical flaws in every major operating system and web browser examined.

The U.K.'s A.I. Security Institute found Mythos succeeded in expert level hacking tasks seventy-three percent of the time. Prior to April 2025, no A.I. model could complete such tasks at all. Of the critical faults discovered, ninety-nine percent remain unpatched.

Rather than releasing Mythos publicly, Anthropic is limiting access through Project Glasswing to organizations like Microsoft, Google, and Apple for defensive cybersecurity testing.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Also in Insights and Trends, new research from the University of Maryland challenges widespread claims about A.I. driven job losses. According to Newswise, the U.M.D. LinkUp A.I. Maps project analyzed one hundred fifty-five million U.S. job postings since 2018.

The findings are notable. A.I. related job postings rose from less than one third of one percent in 2022 to more than one percent by 2025. Overall job postings remain above pre-pandemic levels, with no empirical correlation between increased A.I. adoption and declining job opportunities economy-wide.

Entry level positions reached six percent of total postings in 2025, the highest level in eight years excluding the post-pandemic hiring surge. Professor Anil K. Gupta stated that when looking at economy-wide data, A.I. is not shrinking the labor market but reshaping it. Demand for fresh graduates has not only held up but has strengthened in the A.I. era.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Ethical A.I. today, a Tennessee bill aimed at regulating A.I. safety has advanced after significant changes following White House review. According to StateScoop, the Artificial Intelligence Public Safety and Child Protection Transparency Act originally required large A.I. companies to publish safety plans addressing catastrophic risks.

An analyst told a state advisory council that the White House incorporated feedback that narrowed the bill's scope. The revised version focuses on frontier developers earning more than five hundred million dollars in A.I. revenue and chatbots generating twenty-five million dollars annually with at least one million monthly users.

The amendments carved out exemptions for chatbots used in video games, customer service, and academic research. The bill advanced to the Senate Commerce and Labor Committee following Wednesday's floor vote.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Case Study today, a philosophy professor at Notre Dame is finding a receptive audience among A.I. developers. According to N.P.R., Meghan Sullivan has spent twenty-five years training for conversations about ethics that Silicon Valley is now ready to have.

Sullivan's work is supported by a fifty point eight million dollar grant from the Lilly Endowment designated to advance philosophy and theology in national A.I. ethics discussions. Rather than lecturing, she employs the Socratic method, posing questions that help developers recognize unexplored possibilities.

In March 2026, Sullivan attended Anthropic's summit where Christian leaders discussed how Claude should handle morally complex situations, including appropriate responses to grieving users and those at risk of self harm.

<break time="1.0s"/>

That's today's Innovation Pulse. Thank you for joining us. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.
